title: Why You'd Never Survive a Night on the Moon
screen_title: Why You'd Never Survive a Night on the Moon
subtitle: Two weeks of darkness, 384,000 km from home
yt_title: Why You'd Never Survive a Night on the Moon
intro: The Moon is the only other world humans have walked on. But a single lunar night lasts about two weeks, at around minus 130 degrees Celsius. We land on the Moon and face its airless sky, burning days, freezing nights, sharp dust, radiation and moonquakes, and find out how the next astronauts plan to survive there.
questions: Would you volunteer to spend a night on the Moon?
Did you know a lunar night lasts about two weeks?
What should we never get close to next?
tags: what if you lived on the moon

segments.text: Twelve people have walked on the Moon. Not one of them ever spent a night there. Because a night on the Moon lasts about two weeks, and it's colder than anywhere on Earth. Could you survive it?

files: A Man on the Moon, AS11-40-5903 (cropped).jpg
visual.query: Apollo astronaut Moon

segments.text: Welcome to Next Stop: Universe. If you enjoy calm, easy-to-follow journeys through space, tap subscribe. Today we land on the Moon, and stay for the night.

segments.text: The Moon is about three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away. The Apollo astronauts got there in about three days.
Between nineteen sixty-nine and nineteen seventy-two, twelve astronauts walked on its surface. The longest stay lasted about three days, during the lunar daytime.

files: Aldrin Apollo 11.jpg
visual.query: Aldrin Apollo 11

segments.headline: Only in daylight

segments.text: The Moon turns very slowly. One full day and night, from sunrise to sunrise, takes about twenty-nine and a half Earth days.

files: LADEE Above Lunar Sunset Artist's Concept (9674483648).jpg
visual.query: LADEE Above Lunar Sunset Artist's Concept (9674483648)

segments.headline: A month-long day

segments.text: That means about two weeks of sunlight, followed by about two weeks of darkness.
Where did the Moon come from? Most scientists think that about four and a half billion years ago, a planet about the size of Mars smashed into the young Earth.

files: Earth, Moon and Lunar Module, AS11-44-6643.jpg
visual.query: Earth, Moon and Lunar Module, AS11-44-6643

segments.headline: A giant impact

segments.text: The debris from that collision gathered into a ball in orbit. That ball became our Moon.

files: Moon over Horizon - ISS - August 30 2026 (55502157806).jpg
visual.query: Moon over Horizon - ISS - August 30 2026 (55502157806)

segments.headline: Our Moon is born

segments.text: And it's still moving away from us, about three point eight centimeters every year. We measure it with mirrors the Apollo astronauts left behind.
Let's land in the morning. You step out, and the first thing you notice is the silence. With no air, there's no sound at all.

files: Apollo 14 Lunar Module (LM) on the moon.jpg
visual.query: Apollo 14 Lunar Module (LM) on the moon

segments.headline: Silence

segments.text: And the sky is black, even with the Sun shining. With no air to scatter sunlight, you'd see the Sun and the stars at the same time, if your eyes could adjust.

files: A Man on the Moon, AS11-40-5903 (cropped).jpg
visual.query: A Man on the Moon, AS11-40-5903 (cropped)

segments.headline: A black sky at noon

segments.text: Without a spacesuit, you'd lose consciousness in about fifteen seconds. There's simply nothing to breathe.
By midday, the ground near the equator heats up to around one hundred twenty degrees Celsius. Hotter than boiling water.

files: Apollo 17 Harrison H. Schmitt and Tracy's Rock - AS17-140-21493+AS17-140-21497 2025.jpg
visual.query: Apollo 17 Harrison H. Schmitt and Tracy's Rock - AS17-140-21493+AS17-140-21497 2025

segments.headline: Burning days

segments.text: With no air to carry the heat away, your suit must cool you with water and radiators, or you'd overheat.
Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth of Earth's. A person who weighs sixty kilograms at home would feel like ten.
That's why the Apollo astronauts hopped like kangaroos. Walking normally was harder than bouncing. Some fell over, and laughed, and got back up.

files: Aldrin Apollo 11.jpg
visual.query: Aldrin Apollo 11

segments.headline: Hopping like kangaroos

segments.text: And there's radiation. With no thick air and no magnetic field, the Moon is exposed to the solar wind, cosmic rays, and the full blast of solar storms.

files: Full disk of the Sun (eso1703e-comparisona).jpg
visual.query: Full disk of the Sun (eso1703e-comparisona)

segments.headline: No shield

segments.text: Here's my first question. Would you volunteer to spend a whole night on the Moon? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Would you volunteer to spend a night on the Moon?

segments.text: Then comes the dust. Moon dust isn't like dust on Earth. With no wind or water to wear it down, every grain is sharp, like tiny shards of glass.

files: Apollo 17 Harrison H. Schmitt and Tracy's Rock - AS17-140-21493+AS17-140-21497 2025.jpg
visual.query: Apollo 17 Harrison H. Schmitt and Tracy's Rock - AS17-140-21493+AS17-140-21497 2025

segments.headline: Shards of glass

segments.text: It clung to everything on the Apollo missions. It scratched visors, jammed zippers, and wore through boots.

files: Aldrin Apollo 11.jpg
visual.query: Aldrin Apollo 11

segments.headline: It sticks to everything

segments.text: When astronauts took off their helmets inside the lunar module, the dust smelled like spent gunpowder. Harrison Schmitt of Apollo seventeen even got a kind of hay fever from it.

files: Apollo 17 Harrison H. Schmitt and Tracy's Rock - AS17-140-21493+AS17-140-21497 2025.jpg
visual.query: Apollo 17 Harrison H. Schmitt and Tracy's Rock - AS17-140-21493+AS17-140-21497 2025

segments.headline: Lunar hay fever

segments.text: Breathing it in for months could damage your lungs. Keeping it outside will be one of the hardest jobs for future Moon bases.

files: LUNAR RECEIVING LABORATORY (LRL) - CLARK, ROBERT, DR - JSC (S73-36161).jpg
visual.query: LUNAR RECEIVING LABORATORY (LRL) - CLARK, ROBERT, DR - JSC (S73-36161)

segments.text: Now the Sun sets. And for the next two weeks, there's only darkness.

files: LADEE Above Lunar Sunset Artist's Concept (9674483648).jpg
visual.query: LADEE Above Lunar Sunset Artist's Concept (9674483648)

segments.headline: Sunset

segments.text: Near the equator, the temperature drops to around minus one hundred thirty degrees Celsius.
In some craters near the poles, which never see sunlight at all, it gets even colder, below minus two hundred thirty. Among the coldest places in the whole solar system.

files: AS08-12-2048 - Apollo 8 - Apollo 8 Mission image, Farside of Moon - NARA - 16668536.jpg
visual.query: AS08-12-2048 - Apollo 8 - Apollo 8 Mission image, Farside of Moon - NARA - 16668536

segments.headline: Even colder craters

segments.text: For a machine, the night is the real killer. Batteries freeze, electronics crack, and there's no sunlight for solar panels for two whole weeks.

files: Chang'e 4 Lander- A Closer Look (02 m1147290066lr m130C5A1B).jpg
visual.query: Chang'e 4 Lander- A Closer Look (02 m1147290066lr m130C5A1B)

segments.headline: Machines freeze

segments.text: Many robotic landers simply never wake up after their first night. China's Chang'e landers survive because they carry a small nuclear heat source.

files: Chang'e 4 Lander- A Closer Look (02 m1147290066lr m130C5A1B).jpg
visual.query: Chang'e 4 Lander- A Closer Look (02 m1147290066lr m130C5A1B)

segments.headline: Surviving with nuclear heat

segments.text: For a human, you'd need constant heat, constant power, and enough air, water and food for weeks, with no help nearby.

files: Artemis Lunar Spacesuit Testing (jsc2026e391022).jpg
visual.query: Artemis Lunar Spacesuit Testing (jsc2026e391022)

segments.headline: What you'd need

segments.text: But the lunar night has one gift. Earth hangs in the black sky, glowing blue and white, lighting up the gray ground with earthshine.

files: NASA-Apollo8-Dec24-Earthrise.jpg
visual.query: NASA-Apollo8-Dec24-Earthrise

segments.headline: Earth in the sky

segments.text: And from the near side of the Moon, Earth never rises or sets. It stays almost in the same spot in the sky, slowly changing phase, like a giant blue Moon.

files: The Earth seen from Apollo 17.jpg
visual.query: The Earth seen from Apollo 17

segments.headline: Earth stays still

segments.text: And during a lunar eclipse, seen from the Moon, Earth blocks the Sun. You'd see a glowing red ring around the dark Earth: the light of every sunrise and sunset on our planet, all at once.

files: VLT Cerro Paranal Total Lunar Eclipse 21 December 2010.jpg
visual.query: VLT Cerro Paranal Total Lunar Eclipse 21 December 2010

segments.headline: Every sunset at once

segments.text: The Moon isn't completely quiet, either. Apollo astronauts left seismometers behind, and they recorded moonquakes.

files: Apollo 11 Lunar Laser Ranging Experiment.jpg
visual.query: Apollo 11 Lunar Laser Ranging Experiment

segments.headline: Moonquakes

segments.text: Some shallow moonquakes were strong enough to shake a building on Earth, and lasted for many minutes, because the Moon rings like a bell.

files: Apollo 14 Lunar Module (LM) on the moon.jpg
visual.query: Apollo 14 Lunar Module (LM) on the moon

segments.headline: The Moon rings like a bell

segments.text: And with no air to burn them up, tiny meteorites hit the surface constantly, at tens of kilometers per second. Even a grain of sand could punch a hole in a spacesuit.

files: AS08-12-2048 - Apollo 8 - Apollo 8 Mission image, Farside of Moon - NARA - 16668536.jpg
visual.query: AS08-12-2048 - Apollo 8 - Apollo 8 Mission image, Farside of Moon - NARA - 16668536

segments.headline: Tiny bullets

segments.text: That's also why the Apollo footprints will probably last for millions of years. No wind, no rain. Only the slow rain of micrometeorites will one day erase them.

files: A Man on the Moon, AS11-40-5903 (cropped).jpg
visual.query: A Man on the Moon, AS11-40-5903 (cropped)

segments.headline: Footprints for millions of years

segments.text: Here's my second question. Did you know a single night on the Moon lasts about two weeks? Tell us in the comments.

visual.q: Did you know a lunar night lasts about two weeks?

segments.text: We're still learning new things about the Moon. In June twenty twenty-four, China's Chang'e six mission brought back the first rocks ever collected from the far side, the side we never see from Earth.

files: AS08-12-2048 - Apollo 8 - Apollo 8 Mission image, Farside of Moon - NARA - 16668536.jpg
visual.query: AS08-12-2048 - Apollo 8 - Apollo 8 Mission image, Farside of Moon - NARA - 16668536

segments.headline: Rocks from the far side

segments.text: The far side looks very different, covered in craters, with almost none of the dark lava plains of the near side. Scientists are still figuring out why.

files: AS08-12-2048 - Apollo 8 - Apollo 8 Mission image, Farside of Moon - NARA - 16668536.jpg
visual.query: AS08-12-2048 - Apollo 8 - Apollo 8 Mission image, Farside of Moon - NARA - 16668536

segments.headline: The hidden face

segments.text: So how will the next explorers survive? NASA's Artemis program plans to land astronauts near the Moon's south pole, targeted for twenty twenty-eight.

files: Artemis Lunar Spacesuit Testing (jsc2026e391022).jpg
visual.query: Artemis Lunar Spacesuit Testing (jsc2026e391022)

segments.headline: Artemis

segments.text: Near the pole, some mountain peaks get sunlight almost all the time. And nearby shadowed craters hold water ice: drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel.

files: AS08-12-2048 - Apollo 8 - Apollo 8 Mission image, Farside of Moon - NARA - 16668536.jpg
visual.query: AS08-12-2048 - Apollo 8 - Apollo 8 Mission image, Farside of Moon - NARA - 16668536

segments.headline: Ice and sunlight

segments.text: There may even be water in sunlit places. In twenty twenty, a flying telescope called SOFIA detected water molecules in a large sunlit crater, about as much as a small bottle of water spread through a cubic meter of soil.

files: Apollo 17 Harrison H. Schmitt and Tracy's Rock - AS17-140-21493+AS17-140-21497 2025.jpg
visual.query: Apollo 17 Harrison H. Schmitt and Tracy's Rock - AS17-140-21493+AS17-140-21497 2025

segments.headline: Water in the soil

segments.text: And the soil itself is almost half oxygen by weight, locked in rock. With enough energy, astronauts could squeeze breathable air out of the ground.

files: LUNAR RECEIVING LABORATORY (LRL) - CLARK, ROBERT, DR - JSC (S73-36161).jpg
visual.query: LUNAR RECEIVING LABORATORY (LRL) - CLARK, ROBERT, DR - JSC (S73-36161)

segments.headline: Air from rocks

segments.text: Scientists have also found caves on the Moon, old lava tubes. Living inside one could protect astronauts from radiation, meteorites, and the huge temperature swings.

files: Apollo 14 Lunar Module (LM) on the moon.jpg
visual.query: Apollo 14 Lunar Module (LM) on the moon

segments.headline: Living in caves

segments.text: So, would you survive a night on the Moon? Not without a lot of help. But with the right home, humans may soon stay through their first lunar night.

files: Moon over Horizon - ISS - August 30 2026 (55502157806).jpg
visual.query: Moon over Horizon - ISS - August 30 2026 (55502157806)

segments.headline: The verdict

segments.text: Next time you look at the Moon, remember: someone might be living there in your lifetime.
